--- title: "[Graph.heat_diffusion()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Diffuse heat from seed nodes through the network. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24475-L24621){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.heat_diffusion( seeds, t=1.0, max_iter=50, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Heat diffusion from seed nodes](/assets/graphs/heat-diffusion.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node graph, a diamond A to D joined by the bridge D-E to the triangle E, F, G, with the seed A (node id 1) outlined and every node shaded by the heat it holds after diffusing for time 1. The table reads A 0.31, B and C 0.24, D 0.15, E 0.04, and F and G 0.01: heat fades with distance from the seed and barely crosses the bridge." width="100%"} Places an initial amount of heat on one or more seed nodes and lets it flow along edges according to the heat equation on the graph Laplacian, `dh/dt = -L h`. At every instant each node exchanges heat with its neighbors in proportion to the difference in heat between them, so heat moves from hot nodes to cold ones until it evens out. The result approximates the heat kernel `exp(-t L) h0`, where `h0` is the seed vector. The diffusion time `t=` sets how far heat travels: small values keep it concentrated around the seeds, while large values spread it over the whole connected component until every node holds roughly the same amount. On an undirected graph the total heat is conserved, so the returned values always sum to the total seed heat. Heat diffusion is useful for: - scoring nodes by their network proximity to a set of known "interesting" nodes (e.g., disease genes, flagged accounts, infected hosts) - smoothing a signal defined on a few nodes over their neighborhoods - multi-scale analysis, by comparing results at several values of `t=` Edge weights are ignored; every edge conducts heat equally. For directed graphs, each node exchanges heat only with its successors (out-neighbors), so heat effectively flows against edge direction and the total is generally not conserved. Use an undirected graph if you want the classic, conservative diffusion process. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [seeds]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary mapping seed node IDs (integers) to their initial heat. Every other node starts with zero heat. The values need not sum to `1`: the output scales linearly with them. Must contain at least one entry. IDs that are not in the graph are silently ignored (if none match, every node ends with zero heat). [t]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Diffusion time, which must be positive. Defaults to `1.0`. Larger values let heat spread further from the seeds; as `t=` grows the distribution approaches a uniform spread over each connected component. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[50]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of explicit time steps used to approximate the heat kernel; each step advances time by `t / max_iter`. Defaults to `50`. More steps give a more accurate approximation at proportionally higher cost. The scheme is only numerically stable when the step is small relative to the node degrees (keeping `t / max_iter` at or below `1 / max_degree` is sufficient), so raise `max_iter=` when using a large `t=` or a graph with high-degree hubs. Unstable runs produce oscillating, meaningless values (negative values are clipped to `0`). [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the heat values in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"heat"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the heat values as a dictionary. If `False` (default), return the graph itself for method chaining. In both cases the values are also written to the node DataFrame under `attr_name=`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping every node ID to its heat after diffusion (non-negative floats). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): the graph itself, with the values stored as a node attribute. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `seeds=` is empty or `t=` is not positive. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Here a diamond (A to D) is joined to a triangle (E, F, G) through the single edge D-E. Placing one unit of heat on A and diffusing for the default time leaves most of the heat in the diamond; only a trickle crosses the bridge, and the values still sum to `1`: ::: {#aed6698e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G"), ] ) ) a_id = graph.get_id_from_label("A") heat = graph.heat_diffusion(seeds={a_id: 1.0}, return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): round(h, 3) for nid, h in sorted(heat.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 0.315, 'B': 0.236, 'C': 0.236, 'D': 0.149, 'E': 0.041, 'F': 0.012, 'G': 0.012} ``` ::: ::: The diffusion time controls the reach. With `t=0.2` most of the heat is still on the seed and F and G receive essentially nothing, while with `t=5.0` the heat has nearly evened out across all seven nodes: ::: {#d1ae9e31 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} short = graph.heat_diffusion(seeds={a_id: 1.0}, t=0.2, return_dict=True) long = graph.heat_diffusion(seeds={a_id: 1.0}, t=5.0, return_dict=True) { graph.get_label_from_id(nid): (round(short[nid], 3), round(long[nid], 3)) for nid in sorted(short) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'A': (0.696, 0.172), 'B': (0.138, 0.167), 'C': (0.138, 0.167), 'D': (0.025, 0.153), 'E': (0.002, 0.122), 'F': (0.0, 0.11), 'G': (0.0, 0.11)} ``` ::: ::: Several seeds can be heated at once. Seeding both ends of the graph and storing the result under a custom column name makes it available in the node DataFrame: ::: {#fe77b10c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g_id = graph.get_id_from_label("G") graph.heat_diffusion(seeds={a_id: 1.0, g_id: 1.0}, attr_name="heat_both_ends") graph.get_node_df().select(["label", "heat_both_ends"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
